summary: Analyzes security issues around DDP and RDMAP. It defines an architectural model for an RNIC, reviews attacks on its resources, and describes countermeasures. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A list of ways that fast memory-sharing could be attacked, and ways to protect it.

subtitle: A threat analysis of RDMA network cards: what attackers can do to DDP and RDMAP, and the countermeasures that are required.

tldr.problem: RDMA lets a remote machine place data directly into a host's memory buffers, which gives attackers new ways to read, overwrite or exhaust resources that ordinary stream or datagram networking does not expose.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an architectural model of an RDMA-aware NIC (RNIC), then walks through attacks from the network, from remote peers and from local software, pairing each with countermeasures and MUST or SHOULD requirements for the RNIC and the upper layer protocol.
tldr.outcome: An implementation that follows the recommended mitigations should not exhibit security vulnerabilities beyond those of TCP or SCTP and the protocols beneath them. IPsec is the mandatory-to-implement security framework, and TLS layered on DDP or RDMAP is not recommended.

facts.label: Attack categories
facts.value: Spoofing, tampering, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege

facts.label: Resource Manager role
facts.value: Allocates scarce resources; never sends or receives data

today: RFC 5042 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2007 and has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 7146. Its IPsec requirements are based on the version of IPsec in RFC 2401, as profiled by RFC 3723, and the text says that profile may be updated to the newer IPsec of RFC 4301 in the future.

sections.title: Why RDMA Needs a Security Analysis
sections.content:
Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) gives two parties more flexibility than a stream or datagram model, and the RFC says this flexibility brings new security issues. Those issues matter both to designers of Upper Layer Protocols (ULPs), which may be an application or a middleware library, and to implementers of RDMA-aware NICs (RNICs). An RNIC may implement RDMAP (RFC 5040) and DDP (RFC 5041), or just DDP.

The document first builds an architectural model, then defines which resources can be shared between Streams, then analyzes attacks. Attacks are grouped into those that need end-to-end security to stop, those launched by Remote Peers, and those launched by Local Peers. The categories are spoofing, tampering, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege.

The RFC does not separate a Remote Peer from a Remote ULP, because the source of an attack is often hard to know and the required mitigations are the same either way. It sets a goal: an implementation that uses the recommended mitigations should not have additional vulnerabilities beyond those of TCP or SCTP and the protocols beneath them.
sections.eli5: Letting another computer write straight into your memory is fast, but it also gives bad guys new tricks. This document lists the tricks and how to stop them.

sections.title: The RNIC Architectural Model
sections.content:
The model has four components: the RNIC Engine that implements the protocol, a Privileged Resource Manager that allocates RNIC resources but never sends or receives data, a Privileged ULP and a Non-Privileged ULP. A Privileged ULP is trusted not to attack the local system, though not to allocate resources fairly, for example a kernel ULP. A Non-Privileged ULP is assumed to be untrusted, so anything it does that could affect other ULPs must go through a trusted intermediary. A design goal of DDP and RDMAP is to let a Non-Privileged ULP send and receive directly with the RNIC Engine, under constrained conditions, while the host stays secure.

DDP moves data in two ways. In Untagged Data Transfer, an incoming payload consumes the first buffer in the receiver's queue. In Tagged Data Transfer, the sender names the destination buffer with an STag. For RDMAP these correspond to Send Type Messages and to RDMA Read and RDMA Write Messages.

The RFC lists the resources an attacker may target. For RDMAP all apply; for DDP all but the RDMA Read Request Queue apply. Four interfaces can be exercised: the Privileged Control Interface, the ULP Control Interface, the Non-Privileged Data Transfer Interface and the Privileged Data Transfer Interface. The model is an abstraction, and a real implementation may draw the component boundaries differently while the analysis still applies.

The Protection Domain deserves a note. It is a local construct that is never visible on the wire, and the RNIC checks it before acting on a resource. It ensures an STag can only be used on Streams in the same Protection Domain as the STag.
sections.eli5: Think of a building with a front desk. Visitors can drop packages in their own room, but only the front desk hands out rooms and keys, so nobody can wander into someone else's room.

sections.title: Trust, Sharing and Attacker Capabilities
sections.content:
The RFC assumes that Local and Remote Peers are generally untrusted. Sharing resources between Streams reduces the number of resources needed, but it also allows more attacks. The new term Partial Mutual Trust describes a collection of Streams whose endpoints are willing to assume that none of them will attack the others. ULPs control membership through tools described in Appendix C.

Two requirements follow. All Non-Privileged ULP interactions with the RNIC Engine that could affect other ULPs MUST go through the Privileged Resource Manager as a proxy, and all requests for scarce resources MUST also go through it. The Privileged Resource Manager MUST NOT assume Streams share Partial Mutual Trust unless a mechanism, such as explicit notification from the owning ULP, ensures it.

On the network side, RDMAP and DDP need an LLP Stream set up first, which takes at least one round-trip handshake. An attacker who is not the original Remote Peer either can only send, in which case it must first guess the current LLP Stream parameters such as the TCP sequence number, or can send and receive. An attacker that can pose as each side to the other is a man-in-the-middle, and its breadth of attack is essentially that of the Remote Peer that set up the Stream.
sections.eli5: Friends in the same club may agree not to prank each other, but you should never just assume it. A grown-up at the front desk checks who is really in the club before sharing anything.

sections.title: Network Attacks and End-to-End Security
sections.content:
Some attacks can only be stopped with end-to-end security. In impersonation, a blind attacker must inject a valid transport segment (for TCP, match the 4-tuple and guess a sequence number in the window) and also guess RDMAP or DDP parameters such as the STag and Tagged Offset. An invalid STag tears the Stream down, and because the offset often starts at zero, overwriting an Advertised Buffer mostly comes down to guessing the STag, which should be chosen at random. In Stream hijacking, the attacker waits until authentication succeeds, for example iSCSI authentication, then takes over the Stream. A man-in-the-middle who finds an exposed buffer can read it with RDMA Read, change it with RDMA Write or invalidate the STag.

The defenses are Stream confidentiality against eavesdropping, per-packet data source authentication, per-packet integrity and packet sequencing against replay. If a Stream may face impersonation or hijacking, the RFC recommends it be authenticated, integrity protected and protected from replay, with confidentiality added if it crosses a public network.

On the choice of mechanism the RFC is firm. An RNIC MUST follow the requirements in RFC 3723 Sections 2.3 and 5, so IPsec ESP mode is normative. TLS is not recommended on top of RDMAP or DDP, for two reasons. Under RDMAP, TCP would have to gather out-of-order packets before TLS can decrypt them, which defeats the flow-through design with little to no buffering. On top of RDMAP or DDP, TLS does not protect the headers, so a man-in-the-middle can still steer data into the wrong buffer. DTLS is not chosen because the initial adopters, iSCSI and NFSv4, are compatible with IPsec but use neither TLS nor DTLS.

Receiving an IKE Phase 2 delete message MUST NOT be read as a reason to tear down a DDP/RDMA Stream. IPsec also has to run end-to-end: with a tunnel in the middle of the network, hosts between the Peer and the tunnel device can freely attack the unprotected Stream.
sections.eli5: If someone can read or swap the notes passing between two friends, only a secret code that both share can stop them. The document says to use the IPsec code, not TLS, for this job.

sections.title: Attacks from Remote Peers
sections.content:
The Remote Peer attacks come in several groups. For spoofing, the concern is a Remote Peer using an STag on a different Stream. The cure is either one Protection Domain per Stream, or limiting an STag's scope to a single Stream. An RNIC MUST ensure a Stream cannot use an STag from another Protection Domain or a single-Stream STag from another Stream. STags should be hard to predict and reused as slowly as possible.

For tampering, the RNIC MUST apply a base and bounds check at byte granularity so an RDMA Write or Read Response cannot touch memory outside the buffer behind the STag. A Remote Peer may also modify a buffer after saying it is ready, so the local ULP SHOULD revoke remote access, or check that the peer used Remote Invalidate, before validating the contents. After revocation the RNIC MUST ensure packets using that STag can no longer modify the buffer.

For information disclosure, the ULP SHOULD ensure no stale data is in a buffer before granting remote read access, for example by zeroing it. It SHOULD set base and bounds to expose only the intended data. A buffer meant for remote write MUST be set to enable only remote write, though zero-length RDMA Reads stay permitted. A ULP whose Remote Peers lack Partial Mutual Trust MUST NOT grant write access to the same buffer through different STags.

Denial of service gets the longest treatment, since RNIC resources are valuable and scarce. All allocation of scarce resources MUST be under a Privileged Resource Manager, which can stop unfair use and spot a peer opening too many Streams. Idle Streams can be reaped. Where receive buffers are shared, the RFC suggests low-water and high-water notifications, and the RNIC and Resource Manager MUST be able to detect a peer using more than its fair share. A shared Completion Queue needs a Privileged Resource Manager and sizing so it cannot overflow. RDMA Read Request Queues MUST NOT be shared between Streams without Partial Mutual Trust, and an RNIC SHOULD be able to cap outstanding RDMA Read Requests. A ULP MUST NOT enable an STag valid across multiple Streams without Partial Mutual Trust, because one peer could remotely invalidate it. If a CQ overflows, Streams that do not use it MUST remain unaffected.

Elevation of privilege is treated as a local implementation issue and out of scope.
sections.eli5: A visitor might peek into rooms they should not, scribble on papers after you said they were done, or hog all the chairs. The rules are: check the room number, lock the door when done, and make sure one visitor cannot use up every chair.

sections.title: Attacks from Local Peers
sections.content:
Local attackers are mainly ULPs on the same host. A local ULP that is slow to reap completions on a shared CQ could stall every other ULP using it, and an attacker can also cause entries to be consumed through the Send Queue or Receive Queue. So an RNIC MUST NOT enable sharing a CQ across ULPs that do not share Partial Mutual Trust.

Access to interfaces that allocate RDMA Read Request Queue entries MUST be limited to a trusted Local Peer such as the Privileged Resource Manager, which SHOULD stop a ULP taking more than its fair share.

If a Non-Privileged ULP could write the Page Translation Table directly, it could point it at another ULP's buffers. When Non-Privileged ULPs are supported, the Privileged Resource Manager MUST verify the ULP has the right to access a Data Buffer before allowing an STag to be associated with it.
sections.eli5: Even people living in your own house can take more than their share. A house manager decides who gets what and checks that nobody opens a drawer that is not theirs.

sections.title: Server Guidance and Trust Models
sections.content:
Appendix A is normative and restates the rules for a ULP server that talks to many clients who do not trust each other. Several earlier SHOULDs become MUSTs there. Before operating on a buffer written by a Remote Peer, the server MUST make it impossible to modify by invalidating the STag. A server MUST also make sure no stale data is in a buffer before remote read is granted.

Appendix B is informative and lists which sections place requirements on the RNIC and which on the ULP. Appendix C, also informative, defines five trust models along three questions: are local resources shared, do the local ULPs trust each other, and does the local ULP trust the Remote Peer. NS-NT and S-NT are typical for Internet networking. S-T suits a distributed application on a cluster, and NS-RT is called probably the least likely to be used.

Section 8, the formal security considerations section, simply points to Sections 5, 6 and 7. The IANA section says IANA considerations are not addressed by this document.
sections.eli5: A busy shop owner has the strictest rules because strangers walk in all day. A team working together can relax a little, but only if everyone really is on the team.

viz.caption: RNIC RESOURCES THAT CAN BE ATTACKED (RFC 5042, SECTION 2.2)

items.title: Stream Context Memory
items.text: Per-Stream state, including the Receive Queue and Send Queue.

items.title: Data Buffers
items.text: Exposed untagged for Send Type Messages, or tagged through STags.

items.title: Page Translation Tables
items.text: Map a ULP buffer address to physical addresses.

items.title: Protection Domain
items.text: Local construct, never visible on the wire.

items.title: STag namespace
items.text: A 32-bit name space; the usable space may be much smaller than 2^32.

items.title: Completion Queues
items.text: Tell the ULP that sending or receiving finished.

items.title: Asynchronous Event Queue
items.text: Bounded queue from the RNIC to the Privileged Resource Manager.

items.title: RDMA Read Request Queue
items.text: Holds Read Requests whose responses are not yet fully sent.

data.title: Minimum CQ size
data.code:
ULP trusted to post fewer than the queue size:
  CQ_MIN_SIZE = SUM(MaxPostedOnEachRQ)
              + SUM(MaxPostedOnEachSRQ)
              + SUM(MaxPostedOnEachSQ)

ULP may fill the queues or cannot be trusted:
  CQ_MIN_SIZE = SUM(SizeOfEachRQ)
              + SUM(SizeOfEachSRQ)
              + SUM(SizeOfEachSQ)
